final_answer:
Antibiotic resistance arises through the evolutionary mechanism of natural selection. Bacteria, like all organisms, undergo random genetic mutations. Some mutations may confer resistance to antibiotics. When antibiotics are introduced into an environment, they kill susceptible bacteria while allowing resistant strains to survive and proliferate. Over time, these resistant bacteria become more prevalent, as they are better adapted to the presence of antibiotics. 

Overprescription accelerates this process by increasing the frequency of antibiotic exposure. This creates selective pressure that favors the survival and reproduction of resistant bacterial strains. Additionally, excessive or inappropriate use of antibiotics can lead to the emergence of multidrug-resistant strains, as bacteria are exposed to multiple drugs and have more opportunities to acquire resistance genes. This reduces the effectiveness of antibiotics over time, making infections harder to treat and increasing public health risks.
